title: Methodology for assessing the accuracy of long-term, annual land cover monitoring at national scale: Experiences from the Land Change Monitoring, Assessment, and Projection (LCMAP) initiative
abstract: Annual land cover monitoring using medium-resolution satellite imagery represents a transition from periodic mapping campaigns to continuous observation systems. This transition introduces accuracy assessment challenges not encountered in one-time mapping efforts, particularly when the initial monitoring period is extended forward in time. These challenges are not addressed in existing guidance, which remains largely framed around the evaluation of maps of a single date or maps showing changes between two dates. We present a set of methodological adaptations to adjust to this evolving paradigm, using as a case study the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Land Change Monitoring, Assessment, and Projection (LCMAP) initiative, which generated annual land cover and land cover change products across the historical Landsat archive. Assessing the accuracy of these products was an essential component of LCMAP and resulted in an extensive reference sample dataset that may be used for accuracy estimation, area estimation, or support in the development of new algorithms or models. We review the LCMAP methodology and highlight challenges encountered and lessons learned that are transferable to other long-term, temporally dense monitoring programs. This framework demonstrates that statistically rigorous assessment can scale to operational annual land cover production, while the experiences of the project clarify where existing good practice guidance should be extended to support the needs of ongoing, continuous land cover monitoring.

title: Extracting sea-ice in the arctic by integrating microwave scattering mechanisms with superpixel-based synergistic constraints
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: High-resolution, fine-scale sea-ice extraction is essential for assessing navigation risk in Arctic shipping routes. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) provides all-weather observations and is therefore a key data source for polar sea-ice classification. However, conventional pixel-level SAR classification methods are vulnerable to speckle noise and often produce fragmented misclassifications, and fine-scale ice-water boundary delineation remains challenging when reliable labelled samples are limited and SAR backscatter responses overlap under complex ice conditions. Here, we propose Microwave-scattering Feature and Superpixel Synergy for Ice Classification (MFSS-IC), a fine-scale sea-ice classification model that integrates microwave scattering mechanisms with superpixel-based synergistic constraints. The model first uses simple non-iterative clustering to reconstruct SAR images into radiometrically homogeneous superpixel objects, and then integrates dual-polarization backscatter intensity, global statistical priors derived from Otsu thresholding, and morphological structural constraints, enabling adaptive suppression of speckle noise and fine delineation of ice-water boundaries at the object scale. Reconstruction of sea-ice distributions from the 2015–2022 Sentinel-1 images over the Arctic Northwest Passage, together with cross-validation, showed that: (1) under complex ice conditions, MFSS-IC achieved an overall accuracy (OA) of 98.90%; its superpixel-based synergistic constraints suppressed local high-frequency noise, maintained the spatial connectivity of sea-ice classification results, and effectively reduced the salt-and-pepper artifacts common in conventional methods; (2) under the same regional evaluation, MFSS-IC achieved the highest Kappa coefficient (0.978) and user’s accuracy (UA; 99.20%) among U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and MFSS-IC; its OA exceeded those of U-Net and DeepLabv3+ by 0.50 and 0.23 percentage points, respectively; and (3) MFSS-IC showed strong spatiotemporal generalization, captured nonlinear interannual oscillations in sea-ice distribution driven by climate forcing, and accurately extracted submesoscale fragmented sea-ice in bottleneck regions of the Northwest Passage. The proposed model improves the spatial representation of submesoscale fragmented sea-ice and provides a more reliable basis for quantitative assessment of navigation risk in polar shipping routes.

title: From granularity to consensus: Mitigating sample defects for Remote Sensing Image–Text Retrieval
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Remote Sensing Image–Text Retrieval (RSITR) aims to retrieve remote sensing images or text descriptions when only one modality is available. Despite recent progress, existing RSITR methods often suffer from sample defects, which cause them to mistakenly treat semantically related pairs as negatives, thereby limiting the benefits of advanced feature representations. To tackle the sample defect issue, we propose a novel Dual-Granularity Consensus-guided False Negative Suppression Network (CFSN 2 ), which jointly improves cross-modal alignment and false negative (FN) learning. First, CFSN 2 extracts momentum-updated feature queues for both global and local representations, enabling temporally coherent and stable similarity estimation. Second, it models dual-granularity similarity distributions via Gaussian Mixture Models and detects potential FNs through probabilistic cross-granularity consensus. Finally, the detected FNs are dynamically reweighted based on their FN confidence, softly suppressing their gradients while preserving informative negatives for a balanced optimization process. Extensive experiments across three datasets show that CFSN 2 achieves strong overall retrieval performance, with R@1 scores of 19.12, 28.96, and 22.86 in image-to-text retrieval, and 15.02, 25.22, and 18.00 in text-to-image retrieval, respectively, compared with 26 baselines.

title: SAMWater: a prompt-guided multimodal framework for transferable water mapping with the segment anything model
Corrigendum to “Single-stage signal Attenuation Diffusion Model for Low-Light Image Enhancement and denoising” [Pattern Recognition 183 (2027) 114918]
Comparison of NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) surface reflectance products with MODIS NBAR
abstract: Frequent surface reflectance measurements at fine spatial resolutions are crucial for land surface monitoring. The NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) project addresses this need by combining data from Landsat and Sentinel-2 missions to provide 30-m surface reflectance products with a global average revisit frequency of 2-3 days. This study evaluates the consistency of the HLS Version 2 (V2.0) product against the established Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Nadir Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function-Adjusted Reflectance (NBAR) dataset. We found a high degree of consistency between HLS and MODIS NBAR, with strong positive correlations across all six common spectral bands (R 2 values: 0.939–0.986). Globally, mean absolute differences (MADs) were generally low, typically under 0.03 for visible bands and below 0.05 for NIR and SWIR bands. However, we observed band-dependent discrepancies, with higher discrepancies in the blue and SWIR1 bands. Spatially, substantial differences were found in polar regions, largely due to isolated snow, ice, and water which are fractional and hard to detect within the coarser MODIS pixels but are filtered out in the HLS data. This finding suggests a potential explanation for past disagreements in vegetation trend analyses involving the use of satellite data of different spatial resolutions, as coarser-resolution datasets may mischaracterize greening trends in areas with partial snow and ice cover. These insights are vital for helping users interpret HLS data more effectively and for refining multi-sensor data fusion methods. Our research also provides a valuable baseline for ongoing quality assessment of the HLS product for applications such as vegetation monitoring, land management, and disaster response.
